entries.title: US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry make travel less predictable as countries cancel flights
entries.summary: The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

The threat of secondary US sanctions is putting pressure on airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies that service Iranian airlines. Some countries have already canceled flights.

US sanctions are pushing Iran's weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo. 

Earlier in September as part of "operation economic outcast," the US Treasury Department targeted Iran's aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and potentially lose access to the US financial system. 

The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies. 

For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington's broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.

Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.

For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.

The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.

For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.

Major Middle East routes canceled

Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously for safety reasons that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia have been seriously disrupted.

On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.

Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.

A passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.

As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the "J-1" general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.

Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.

The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.

More travelers use land crossings

With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.

One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.

"The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close," he told DW anonymously.

For families, elderly passengers, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.

Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.

That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.

Iran's shaky aviation industry

Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions. 

Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.

An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.

When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.

Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran's GDP.

"Iran's aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time," Salavati told DW.

"The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money," Salavati added.

Iran isolated by air and sea

Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.

Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.

If those first connections disappear, Iran's international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.

The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult. 

If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states. 

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar’s immunity, clears way for probes into 2 former Orban ministers
entries.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has backed the move himself. Two former ministers who served under his rival Viktor Orban now face separate corruption probes.
entries.content:
Hungary

Hungary lifts PM Peter Magyar's immunity, ex-Orban ministers

September 28, 2026

Prime Minister Peter Magyar has backed the move himself. Two former ministers who served under his rival Viktor Orban now face separate corruption probes.

Hungary's parliament on Monday lifted Prime Minister Peter Magyar's immunity from prosecution, along with that of two former ministers from Viktor Orban's government.

The votes clear the way for investigations involving Magyar and the two opposition lawmakers, who all face separate allegations.

What did the Hungarian lawmakers decide?

Parliament voted 139-0 to lift the immunity of Magyar, former Culture and Innovation Minister Balazs Hanko and former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. Lawmakers from Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party and its conservative Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP) ally did not take part in the vote.

Magyar, whose center-right Tisza party came to power in April, had himself called on lawmakers to lift his immunity.

Prosecutors are investigating an incident in 2024 in which Magyar allegedly took a mobile phone from a man who was filming him at a Budapest nightclub and threw it into the Danube.

Magyar has described the case as a "farce" and accused prosecutors of trying to associate his case with corruption allegations against former members of Orban's government.

What are the former Orban ministers accused of?

Hanko, now a Fidesz lawmaker, is being investigated over the alleged misuse of public money from Hungary's National Cultural Fund.

Prosecutors allege that public funds were improperly used in more than 1,000 cases, causing losses of 17.3 billion forints (€44.5 million/$52.3 million). Hanko has rejected the allegations.

Sesztak, a KDNP lawmaker who served as national development minister from 2014 to 2018, faces a separate investigation concerning alleged bribes linked to contracts involving the state-owned bus company Volanbusz.

Magyar defeated Orban in April after campaigning on a pledge to investigate alleged corruption and abuses of power during Orban's 16 years in office.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
entries.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.
entries.content:
France

Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit

September 28, 2026

French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.

Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine, located near the Spanish border, is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."

Later, the pope also said it was "impossible to regard causing death as something normal."

"What is legal is not necessarily moral," he added, in what could be seen as a reference to France's euthanasia and assisted suicide law which came into effect last month.

"We must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," said the 71-year-old pontiff.

Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church met with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse — part of the  Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.

A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.

While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."

But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.

"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

 "You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

Pope calls on Europe to help end cycle of 'lies and deceit'

On Monday, speaking in the city of Metz on the last day of his French visit, the pope warned of what he called "increasingly uncivilized" intra-national relations and people boasting about their "lies and deceit."

He called on Europe to "help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve."

The pope's visit to Metz, near the border with Luxembourg and Germany, was to honor Robert Schuman, a French Catholic statesman regarded as one of the founding fathers of European unity.

The US-born pontiff's remarks are in stark contrast with views on Europe voiced by many in the current Trump administration and will be seen by many as an implicit criticism of its political practice.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Wesley Dockery, and Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Turkey: Comedian on trial for 'insulting' Erdogan in show
entries.summary: Deniz Goktas is accused of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, "praising" crime and criminals, and "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey: Comedian on trial for 'insulting' Erdogan in show

September 28, 2026

Deniz Goktas is accused of "insulting" President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, "praising" crime and criminals, and "inciting hatred and hostility" with jokes about Islam. Nominally, Turkey is a secular country with free speech.

A Turkish comedian goes on trial in Istanbul on Monday facing charges of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other offenses during a stand-up performance in June. 

Deniz Goktas, 32, was arrested on July 3, a week after releasing a YouTube video of his show that was watched nearly 9 million times and a few days after shorter clips he posted on X enjoyed similar rapid success. 

A group of around 50 protesters gathered outside the courtroom with umbrellas in pouring rain on Monday morning, chanting "Deniz Goktas is not alone."

Supporters and journalists were also waiting to enter the courtroom, including several fellow comedians from Istanbul's TuzBiber club, and observers from the Dutch embassy and the US consulate.

NATO member and EU aspirant Turkey routinely tries people on speech-related offenses, particularly and famously when it comes to supposed "insults" of its longserving leader Erdogan.

What charges does Goktas face?

Goktas, who has been held in pretrial detention since July, faces an array of charges related to content in his "Dead Sea" show. He referred to his impending court appointment online on Sunday, in one of his irreverent social media posts from his cell.

"After 88 days, I'll be handcuffed for the first time and hear a car horn. I'm definitely not missing the handcuffs, but let's see if I've missed the car horn," he quipped.

Goktas is accused of insulting Erdogan, of inciting public hatred and hostility — via jokes about Islam — and of praising crime and criminals, an addition charge added by prosecutors tied to a joke about an organized crime family, the Daltons

"A 90-minute show spawns a new charge every two months," Goktas wrote in late August, saying they had added the extra charge against him "for a joke about the Daltons."

Because Turkish judges can issue consecutive jail sentences for multiple convictions, rather than them being served concurrently, Goktas could in theory be exposed to several years in prison.

His trial is the latest in a widening crackdown on people seen as critical of Turkey's moderate Islamist government. Hundreds of politicians, artists, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists are among those to face detenion or trial. 

Erdogan the only claimant, Diyanet religious authority among those to complain

According to the Turkish NGO the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA), prosecutors cited more than 500 applications to prosecute the performer regarding the show. 

They were issued to the Presidential Communication Center that monitors such issues. One of the groups to provide a tipoff was the government-sponsored Preidency of Religious affairs, better known as Diyanet.

Erdogan is named as the sole complainant.

The indictment highlights specific jokes from Goktas' show as exceeding the bounds of permissible speech.

Goktas describing Erdogan as a "shy dictator" and saying he had undergone "a transition to a dictator who is at peace with his own identity" are listed as the insults against the man in charge of Turkey, either as prime minister or later as president, since 2003.

Erdogan's government has attracted attention in recent years for its prosecution of people deemed to have unfairly criticized the authorities, and for the various lawsuits against leading members of the opposition, particularly the CHP. The Turkish president's litigious streak also became headline news in Germany around a decade ago, when he pursued star TV comedian Jan Böhmermann.

Meanwhile the MLSA said that Goktas' jokes alleged to have the potential to "publicly incite hatred and hostility" took aim at fundamentalist Islam, including a reference to women in full-coverage swimsuits being "divers" and joking about "suicide bombers who fast."

Turkey nominally has a secular constitution and guarantees of free speech. However, the EU and the US have often criticized its application of these standards.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom wrote in a 2022 report that Erdogan's government increasingly relied on speech-based proseuction to "silence individuals who express criticism in religious terms, disclose beliefs or a lack thereof that differ from those of the majority of the population, or engage with religion in a way perceived as 'mocking' or 'irreverent.'"

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Diesel prices are surging. Ukraine is only part of the story
entries.summary: Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's diesel crunch even worse.
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's diesel crunch even worse.

Even if you don't fill your own vehicle with diesel, its price has a big impact on your life.

While gasoline is mainly a consumer fuel for cars, diesel powers much of the wider economy, from freight transport and farming equipment to construction and industry.

That is why diesel shortages or price shocks can have a bigger economic impact than higher gasoline prices by raising the cost of moving goods and operating heavy machinery.

As businesses become strained, these higher energy costs will be passed on to consumers and add to a growing cost-of-living crisis and inflation. So what's driving global diesel prices higher?

The US blames Ukraine for diesel shortages

The United States and China are among the world's largest diesel producers. China keeps much of it for domestic use, leaving the US as the world's biggest diesel exporter.

Still, the weekly average price of a gallon of diesel is now $6.52 (€5.73) in the country, according to the US Energy Information Administration, a big increase from a year ago when it averaged $3.74 per gallon or two years ago when it averaged $3.53 a gallon.

President Donald Trump recently called on Ukraine's president to stop targeting oil refineries in Russia "because he's causing a shortage of diesel."

Russia is one of the world's other biggest diesel suppliers. But since 2022, some of its oilrefineries have been attacked as many as 15 times, according to the International Energy Agency.

The agency estimates that diesel production in Russia is down by nearly 30% from 2025 levels. Moscow has now restricted diesel exports to protect domestic supplies.

As Russian production declined, the US went into high gear to help make up the difference, but even this was not enough. And on September 22, Trump announced that his administration was also considering a diesel export ban.

Such a move is likely an attempt to bring down domestic prices ahead of the November midterm elections since energy prices and affordability have become important campaign issues.

Leading energy lobby groups have come out against such a plan, and many industry experts think a ban would be slow to bring down prices or could backfire by pushing US refiners to reduce production, push up prices, or both.

Europe is especially vulnerable to diesel shocks

For Europe, more expensive diesel could have dramatic consequences.

"Decades of policy incentives, such as tax advantages, left Europe's vehicle fleet far more diesel-heavy than regions like the US," said Georg Zachmann, a senior fellow at Brussels-based Bruegel think tank.

"As a result, the EU is structurally long on gasoline, which it exports, and short on diesel, which it must import," added Zachmann, who specializes in energy and climate policies.

In the EU, just over 38% of passenger cars are diesel and road transport, including freight, makes up 77% of total diesel and gas oil consumption, according to a briefing published by Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based advocacy group.

This reliance on diesel-powered transport "leaves drivers and businesses particularly exposed to oil and fuel price shocks," wrote Juliette Egal, the briefing's lead author.

The NGO calculated that EU drivers are paying €30 more for a 50-liter tank of diesel on average since the start of the war in Iran. An average German long-haul truck driver is paying an extra €236 a week.

Increased fuel costs for EU road transport add up to €270 million a day — of that, €203 million is for diesel, according to the briefing. Overall, the EU economy has seen additional costs of €40 billion from road diesel since the beginning of the war.

Why are diesel prices climbing faster than oil?

In the near term, Russia's crude oil processing volumes are the single fastest-moving lever, said Skip York, a nonresident fellow at Rice University's Center for Energy Studies in Houston, Texas.

"Each new wave of Ukrainian strikes shows up in diesel prices within days, unlike Hormuz, which has been running at a depressed but relatively stable flow rate for months," he added.

York points out that, perhaps surprisingly, crude oil production, the raw material needed to make diesel and gasoline, isn't the biggest constraint. That is why oil prices have moved modestly while diesel has soared.

"The oil bottleneck has shifted from 'not enough crude' in March/April to 'not enough refining capacity' since August," the expert told DW.

Now refinery disruptions matter most, he said, because "both the Ukraine drone campaign and the Hormuz conflict are knocking out working refining capacity faster than anyone can replace it."

Still, the Strait of Hormuz "is the bigger structural risk" for diesel prices in the long term.

Globally, refinery capacity has "dropped substantially, and diesel is particularly affected," agreed Zachmann.

Where will diesel prices go from here?

Prolonged fighting in the Middle East or Russia could add to the problems for Europe and other diesel users. US export restrictions could make this situation even worse.

US diesel exports to Europe are up around 37% since last year and now account for about 8% of European demand, says York. This makes the country an important alternative to diesel from Russia and the Persian Gulf.

If the US blocks exports, it would be a big shock and mean even higher diesel prices, said Zachmann. The question is whether the EU would retaliate and export less gasoline to the US "making both sides worse off" by pushing up both US gasoline prices and EU diesel prices.

Additionally, winter is just around the corner for the Northern Hemisphere. Refineries may struggle to meet demand for both heating oil and diesel, further tightening supplies.

A wave of refinery closures in Europe and the US since 2019 has made the diesel market vulnerable, said York, and this has hit the buffer of spare refining capacity that used to absorb shocks.

"Essentially, the market has fewer 'extra barrels' standing by," he underscored. "So, the loss of any barrel hits supply much more directly than it used to."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Nations League match overshadowed by political controversy
entries.summary: Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip.
entries.content:
September 28, 2026

Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip.

The Irish team bowed their heads during playing of the Israeli national anthem on Sunday night and they declined to shake hands with their opponents, a gesture that is customary before international fixtures.

Ireland played the match wearing black armbands in memory of those killed in Israel's military operation in the Gaza Strip, and just 24 hours earlier it was unclear whether the match would go ahead at all.

'Significant majority' vote to play

On Saturday, the players voted in favor of playing what was technically a home match for Israel in Debrecen, Hungary, despite widespread opposition to their participation among the Irish public.

David Courell, the chief executive of the Irish FA (FAI), told a press conference that had been delayed for several hours while players and coaches met to discuss the issue, that a significant majority of the squad had voted to play.

"Based on that, the association took ⁠the decision on behalf of Irish ​football that this fixture would continue, as we have always intended to fulfil the fixtures," he said.

However, the vote was not unanimous and one player, reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, decided to pull out of the squad for this and a second match against Israel during this international break.

In Sunday's match, Troy Parrott netted the opener for Ireland in the 14th minute, with ​Adam Idah scoring two minutes later. Jack Moylan added a third in the 25th to make the final score 3-0.

Few supporters present

The fixture was played in a largely empty stadium in Debrecen, with just a few hundred Israeli fans and a handful of Irish supporters in attendance.

The FAI had not reserved any tickets for their fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE showed the match without the usual halftime analysis.

Over the previous few days, the Irish team had been under intense pressure from Irish fans and politicians to boycott the fixture.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause and formally recognized a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway. Dublin has also repeatedly criticized Israel over the Gaza conflict.

A Hamas raid into Israel on October 7, 2023, killed around 1,200 people, prompting Israel's attack on Gaza which has killed over 73,000.

Ireland's next Nations League match was originally scheduled to be played in Dublin on October 4, but due to security concerns, it has been moved to the Serbian town of Backa Topola, where it is to be played behind closed doors.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: Sweden faces political deadlock after election-winning center-left bloc fails to form government
entries.summary: Swedish Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson has abandoned efforts to form a four-party government. Deep divisions within the election-winning bloc have left Sweden in political deadlock.
entries.content:
Sweden

Sweden's center-left bloc fails to form government

September 28, 2026

Swedish Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson has abandoned efforts to form a four-party government. Deep divisions within the election-winning bloc have left Sweden in political deadlock.

The leader of Sweden's center-left Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, on Monday said her talks with other parties had failed to form a government after her bloc's narrow election victory.

The breakdown leaves Sweden without a new government more than two weeks after the election and opens the door for the outgoing right-wing bloc to try to remain in power despite losing the vote.

Why did Sweden's government talks fail?

Andersson had been trying to bring together the Social Democrats, Greens, Center Party and Left Party, which together won 176 of parliament's 349 seats.

But talks foundered on deep divisions between the centrist Center Party and socialist Left Party.

"Based on the discussions I have had, I can conclude that, as things currently stand, it is not possible for me to form a government," Andersson told reporters.

The four-party bloc won 176 seats in the September 13 election, compared with 173 for the outgoing right-wing alliance. The popular vote difference was around 50,000.

What happens next?

The speaker of parliament is now expected to ask another party leader to try to form a government, with outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson of the center-right Moderate Party the likely next choice.

Kristersson continues to lead a caretaker government. His bloc, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats, has also failed to secure a majority and would probably need support from the Center Party.

Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has ruled out supporting a government that gives influence to either the Sweden Democrats or the Left Party.

Protracted government formation is not unusual in Sweden. It took 37 days to establish a government following the 2022 election and 134 days after the vote in 2018.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

Skip next section Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passes resolution seeking urgent restoration of full statehood

Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passes resolution seeking urgent restoration of full statehood

The regional assembly of India-administered Kashmir on Monday passed a resolution seeking the urgent restoration of full statehood from its current status of a Union Territory, which is federally administered. 

The resolution was introduced by Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and was passed in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly amid chaos as legislators of the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staged a walkout calling the non-binding resolution "unconstitutional" and "anti-national".

The resolution calls on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government in New Delhi to ensure "the immediate and urgent restoration of full (federal) statehood to Jammu and Kashmir".

In 2019, a contentious decision by the Modi government stripped Jammu and Kashmir of its semiautonomous status.

The region was divided into two federally administered territories, bringing it directly under New Delhi's control.

In 2024, the region elected its first government since being recategorized as a Union Territory with Abdullah's Jammu and Kashmir National Conference party at its helm.

But the local government's powers are limited.

The Modi government has consistently said that statehood for the territory would be granted at an "appropriate time".

On Monday, Abdullah, who said that statehood was the territory's "right," sought a clarification on the timeline and questioned what "appropriate time" means, local Kashmir outlets reported.

The text of Monday's resolution also referred to the constitutionally non-binding resolutions demanding federal autonomy, passed in 2000 and 2024.

Modi's BJP, which is the largest opposition party in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, strongly opposed the resolution with protests and sloganeering as Abdullah spoke ahead of the vote. BJP legislators also tore up copies of the resolution, reports said.

Muslim-majority Kashmir has long been a bone of contention for India and Pakistan, both of whom lay claim to the restive, strategically important Himalayan region.

Skip next section Chhattisgarh floods: Air Force personnel rescue 12 people stranded on hut roof

Chhattisgarh floods: Air Force personnel rescue 12 people stranded on hut roof

Heavy rains have wreaked havoc in the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh, causing rivers and streams to swell up and leading to flood-like conditions in some parts. 

Over 5,000 people were rescued over the weekend from the inundated areas and taken to relief camps and safer locations, according to reports.

The districts of Bastar, Dhamtari, Bilaspur, Durg, Raipur, Balodabazar-Bhatapara and Narayanpur are among the regions affected by the heavy downpour.

On Monday, the Indian Air Force (IAF) rescued 12 people stranded in a village on the northern bank of the Indravati river, which was flowing above the danger mark, news agency ANI quoted a Defense Ministry statement as saying.

The group of people, which included women and children, were reportedly stuck on the roof of a hut which was at risk of collapsing due to the force of the floodwaters.

An IAF commando was lowered on the roof from a helicopter, which hovered above as the people were pulled up, according to the ministry.

Skip next section India's Supreme Court takes note of recent Delhi-NCR rape cases

India's Supreme Court takes note of recent Delhi-NCR rape cases

The Supreme Court of India said on Monday that the recent slew of rape cases in the Indian capital of New Delhi and its neighboring districts "starkly underline a systematic failure" by law enforcement and public administrative authorities, legal news websites reported.

The top court made the statement as it opened a "suo motu cognizance" legal review of the latest cases of rape in Delhi-National Capital Region (NCR), LiveLaw and Bar and Bench reported.

In Indian law, a suo motu cognizance refers to a court taking notice of a matter on its own initiative, without a formal petition or complaint being filed.

The two-judge bench expressed its distress over the news reports of the recurring sexual violence and underpinned the need to fix accountability, LiveLaw reported.

"These incidents considered alongside other recent reports of sexual offences across Delhi-NCR starkly underline a systematic failure on the part of the law enforcement and the public administrative authorities to guarantee basic public safety," LiveLaw quoted the bench as saying.

Last week, Delhi saw hundreds of students protesting and expressing their outrage over the safety of women after a teenage girl was allegedly gang raped by three men at a public park in the capital.

In August, media reports said that a ​17-year-old ‌girl was allegedly gang raped in a bus moving from Noida, a staellite city of the Indian capital, to Delhi by the vehicle's driver and conductor.

The court on Monday said that public spaces, including parks, roads, buses, metro stations, subways and footbridges, cannot be allowed to become "high-risk zones" over inadequate illumination or surveillance, lack of patrolling, or other preventable administrative inadequacies, Bar and Bench reported.

Supreme court says need to fix accountability

The judges drew parallels with the 2012 fatal Delhi gang rape on a bus that came to be known as the Nirbhaya case.

"One cannot help but draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012," LiveLaw reported the bench as saying.

The court also observed whether the systematic law enforcement apparatus has made any meaningful advancement since the Nirbhaya case, according to LiveLaw.

The court stressed that "expressions of solidarity" were not a solution to the offences it called "social evil," adding that a "measurable response" was required with fixing "responsibility and accountability" upon the authorities entrusted with crime prevention, maintenance of public order and protection of vulnerable persons, according to local outlets.

Skip next section India's badminton star Sindhu 'hurting' after hectic Asian Games schedule

India's badminton star Sindhu 'hurting' after hectic Asian Games schedule

Indian badminton star PV Sindhu has voiced her disappointment at losing her Asian Games quarterfinal, also questioning her gruelling schedule that saw her play three matches in less than 24 hours over the weekend.

"My Asian Games campaign is over, and I'm hurting," Sindhu wrote to her roughly 3 million followers on social media. "I had my chance. Letting it slip hurts."

The 31-year-old lost to China's Chen Yufei on Sunday, having played both her second and third round matches on Saturday.

"Three matches in 18 hours. Back at 3 a.m. [on Saturday night], out again at 8:30 a.m. [on Sunday morning]. It took a toll," the former world champion and two-time Olympic medalist wrote.

Sindhu thanked fans who had stayed up to cheer her on and said she also felt a sense of pride at competing her fourth Asian Games, concluding the post by saying, "I'll go again."

Sindhu's India teammate H.S. Prannoy had similarly criticized both the packed schedule and other conditions for players like accommodation and logisticts in the province of Aichi and main city of Nagoya in Japan.

"It's cruel beacuse everybody is aiming for a good Asian Games, which comes once in four years," Prannoy said. "To have two singles games in a day, I haven't seen it like that in ages."

Skip next section Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault

Lovely Professional University protest: Classes suspended after violence during protests over suspected assault

Punjab's Lovely Professional University (LPU) has suspended classes starting Monday and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported. 

The private university located in the city of Phagwara witnessed massive student unrest after claims spread on social media that a female university student was allegedly raped within the campus premises by an outsider and had later died by suicide.

The protests grew to be violent when the protesters clashed with the police, pelted stones at the security personnel, smashed windows and set fire to some objects within the university complex, reports said.

Some students later claimed in social media posts that the vandals were not students, but outsiders.

Heavy police deployment

The university has suspended regular classes for 10 days, news agency ANI cited a statement from LPU as saying.

The statement said students could travel to their hometowns during the suspension of classes and advised those who stay back to remain in their hostels or places of accommodation and avoid any unnecessary movement. The statement also called on students to avoid involvement in the unrest.

Over 2,000 police personnel were deployed to ensure security on the campus, reports quoted the Additional Director General of Police Fayaz Farooqui as saying.

The protesters also blocked the national highway between Jalandhar and Phagwara highway early Sunday, leading to traffic disruptions.

On Monday, police said that the situation had been brought under control and traffic movement on the highway had been restored.

Claims of rape remain unverified

Meanwhile, the police are yet to confirm whether a student was raped within LPU's campus. They have launched an investigation to examine the facts of the incident.

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has taken note of the situation and has directed the Director General of Police to visit the campus, reports said on Monday.

Meanwhile, the Punjab State Women Commision is seeking a detailed report on the alleged rape, ANi reported.

What has LPU said?

The LPU has denied that the alleged rape took place, calling the claims "false, baseless and fabricated rumors".

The university on Sunday posted a video with three female students who it said reside in the girls' hostel room where the alleged incident is claimed to have taken place.

The video purportedly shows the girls denying that there had been a rape, with one of them asking the police to stop visiting the room repeatedly.

However, media reports on Monday said that the same girls later appear in a separate purported video, claiming that they were instructed on what to say in the statement. They then allegedly claim that their clips were "trimmed" and used without their consent.

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you the Monday edition of our India blog — where we break down all the biggest headlines that have got the world's most populous nation talking.

Weather seems to be going through a changing mood in the northern, central and eastern parts of India. There is a nip in the air in the Indian capital and surrounding regions, heavy rains have led to a flood-like situation unfolding in the state of Chhattisgarh, while lofty sections of the Himalayan states of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are witnessing a snowfall.

On the other hand, heat is on in the state of Punjab — quite literally — after massive student unrest at a private university, over rumors of a rape on campus, saw protesters damaging property on the university premises and torching some objects.

Meanwhile, India's top court has started a legal review of the recent rape cases in Delhi and the National Capital Region, drawing parallels to the 2012 Nirbhaya rape case that became a symbol of the country's battle against sexual violence, leading to sweeping legal reforms.

The Supreme Court has now questioned if systemic law enforcement mechanisms have actually made any meaningful progress, nearly 14 years on.

Stay tuned as we bring you more.

entries.title: Venezuelans demand opposition leader Machado's return
entries.summary: Hundreds of people held rallies in Venezuela demanding the safe return of Maria Corina Machado, and fair elections.
entries.content:
Venezuela

Venezuelans demand opposition leader Machado's return

September 28, 2026

Hundreds of people held rallies in Venezuela demanding the safe return of Maria Corina Machado, and fair elections.

Supporters of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado held a rally on Sunday demanding her safe return and for fair presidential elections in Venezuela.

Her supporters joined the rally wearing sky-blue shirts which is the color of Machado's Vente Venezuela party and rode motorcycles through the streets in Caracas.

Similar rallies were held in several state capitals including Valencia, Maracaibo and Merida.

"This is not a matter of parties or politics," said Flavio Valentini, a Vente Venezuela activist in Caracas who grabbed a megaphone and addressed the crowd.

"This is a movement for the people and by the people."

The demonstrators demanded a clear timeline for presidential elections in 2027 and chanted slogans including "Freedom, freedom!"

Machado's return from exile

For the past nine months, Machado has been living in exile. Last year in December, Machado left for Oslo to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then she has tried returning to Venezuela multiple times.

Machado, who is currently in Panama, has so far made seven unsuccessful attempts to return, according to media reports.

Activists allege the Venezuelan government keeps blocking her return, however, Venezuelan authorities deny the claim.

Courts had barred Machado from running in elections under the government of President Nicolás Maduro. But her stand-in candidate is widely believed to have won the election.

Maduro refuted the election results. After his disputed victory, his government led a crackdown against dissidents who protested the official results, forcing Machado and dozens of opposition leaders to flee.

The US captured Maduro in January. But Machado has been unable to return to Venezuela since then.

Currently, the country is being led by acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who has worked closely with Washington.

"We hope this transition process leads us to presidential elections and consolidates a free, democratic country that will be the main ally of the United States," said Anthony Romero, a leader for Vente Venezuela in the nation's capital.
